title: Work Backwards
coreInsight: When a forward process compounds complexity, reversing invertible steps can expose the starting state much more directly.
narrativeTransition: Give the learner a final machine output and make forward guessing visibly inefficient, then reverse each operation in the opposite order.
commonMisconceptions: Inverse operations can be applied in the same order as the forward process.
Every output has exactly one predecessor.
A backward candidate need not be verified by running it forward.
Working backwards means algebraically rearranging every problem regardless of structure.

title: Logic & Constraint Elimination
coreInsight: Every clue removes possibilities; a solution is justified only when all constraints hold and competing possibilities are eliminated.
narrativeTransition: Begin with a small visible universe of possibilities and let each clue cross out states, making logical deduction feel like shrinking a feasible set.
commonMisconceptions: Clues may be used independently without checking their interaction.
The converse of a statement is automatically true.
Finding one candidate is enough without checking uniqueness.
Unstated assumptions from a diagram or story can be treated as constraints.

title: Parity & Invariants
coreInsight: Instead of tracking every detail of a process, track a coarse property that remains fixed or changes predictably.
narrativeTransition: Run a complicated sequence of moves while coloring only an odd/even or other invariant state so the preserved structure stays visible while everything else changes.
commonMisconceptions: Matching parity means two numbers are equal.
Any simple quantity is useful to track even if it is not preserved.
Parity arguments require computing exact values first.

title: Pigeonhole & Guaranteed Outcomes
coreInsight: Worst-case distribution can prove what must eventually happen even when the exact arrangement is unknown.
narrativeTransition: Ask how long the desired event can be avoided, fill every category as adversarially as possible, and identify the next object as the forced step.
commonMisconceptions: A likely or average-case outcome is a guarantee.
The desired event is forced as soon as every category has at least one item.
The distribution should be assumed balanced rather than constructed as a worst case.
Pigeonhole arguments require knowing the exact arrangement.
